protocol.instrument_name: Hormonal Contraception Clinical Practice Protocol - Tasmanian Community Pharmacist Program
protocol.instrument_version: Version 1.0 (cover: 'Version 1.0 October 2025'; authority table: 'V1.0 October 2025 Dale Webster Secretary, Department of Health'; prepared by Duncan McKenzie, Program Director, Pharmacy Projects 24 November 2025)
protocol.effective_date: October 2025 (cover and version history); authorised by Dale Webster, Secretary, Department of Health 26 November 2025
protocol.legal_basis: Authorisation Statement (page 3): 'In accordance with Tasmanian Poisons Regulations 2018 Regulation 7(4) - I authorise this protocol.' (signed by the Secretary, Dale Webster). Relevant Legislation (page 4): 'Regulation 7: (4) A pharmacist, in the lawful practice of the pharmacist's profession, may possess, sell, supply or prescribe any scheduled substance in accordance with a protocol authorised by the Secretary, that specifically authorises the possession, sale, supply or prescription of that substance by a pharmacist. This protocol has been authorised by the Secretary.' About (page 4): 'It is a regulatory requirement under the Tasmanian Poison Regulations 2018 that pharmacists follow this protocol under a structured prescribing arrangement.' Background (page 4): 'A change to the Poisons Regulations 2018 allows pharmacists to prescribe medications according to a protocol authorised by the Secretary of Health.' Issuing a prescription (page 20): 'Any prescription needs to comply with Regulation 45 of the Tasmanian Poisons Regulations 2018 which outlines the elements needed to produce a valid prescription in Tasmania.'
protocol.supervision_model: Structured prescribing arrangement under a protocol authorised by the Secretary of Health. About (page 4): pharmacists 'must only offer this structured prescribing service in a pharmacy premises that has been approved for this purpose by the Department of Health and meets the conditions outlined within this protocol in Amenities and resource requirements.' Conditions (page 5): the pharmacist 'has successfully completed a hormonal contraception training program that meets criteria defined by this protocol'; must 'take all reasonable steps to prescribe contraceptives in accordance with the current online version of the section of the Therapeutic Guidelines titled Sexual and Reproductive Health: Contraception'; must make a written prescription compliant with regulation 45; must make an individualised clinical assessment and 'make and retain an electronic clinical record of the consultation'; and 'must not prescribe, in one prescription, greater than 12 months' supply.' Training must be delivered by a TEQSA-accredited higher education institution or a training provider meeting the Australian Pharmacy Council's 'Standards for Continuing Professional Development Activities' (page 6).
protocol.scope_summary: Tasmanian Department of Health clinical practice protocol (Version 1.0, October 2025) authorising appropriately trained community pharmacists to prescribe hormonal contraception to patients aged 16 years or over. Permitted medicines (Conditions, page 5): combined hormonal contraception - combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) and the contraceptive vaginal ring, 'Excluding preparations containing 50 micrograms or more of ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol'; progestogen-only contraceptive pill; depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (injection). Protocol Overview (page 7) sequences six stages: meet service and professional obligations (initial eligibility and suitability, informed consent); patient history and assessment (sexual, reproductive and social history, sexual and reproduction health counselling, exclude pregnancy, examination incl. BMI and BP measurement); contraceptive and sexual health plan (discuss LARCs; select COC, combined hormonal vaginal ring, POP or DMPA); confirm contraception plan is appropriate (UKMEC; contraindications, precautions and interactions; pregnancy and lactation); communicate agreed contraception plan (medication counselling, general advice and patient information, communication with other health practitioners); clinical review (measure BP and BMI, adverse effects, continue/change/stop contraception, communication with other health professionals). Page 8 lists seven 'Refer when' situations and four 'Treat and concurrently refer promptly' situations. Pregnancy must be reasonably excluded before commencing any hormonal contraception using an all-AND plus any-of-five decision rule, with referral if any doubt remains (page 11). The UK MEC calculator must be used; MEC 1 or 2 may be prescribed, MEC 3 or 4 must be referred to an alternative prescriber (page 14) and 'CANNOT be prescribed as part of the Hormonal Contraception Service' (page 18). Combined hormonal contraception may be initiated only at ages 16-40; ages 41-50 may only continue existing combined hormonal contraception with one original manufacturer's pack and concurrent GP review, and initiation is not permitted in that age group (page 15). Clinical review 3 months after initiation of a new method and 12-monthly thereafter; total quantity prescribed including repeats must not exceed 12 months' supply (pages 19-20). Page 17 contains no extractable text.

inclusion.text: Condition 1: 'A pharmacist practising in a Tasmanian community pharmacy who has successfully completed a hormonal contraception training program that meets criteria defined by this protocol may prescribe the following medicines to a patient aged 16 years or older: a) Combined hormonal contraception - combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) and the contraceptive vaginal ring. Excluding preparations containing 50 micrograms or more of ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol. b) Progestogen-only contraceptive pill c) Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (injection)'

Condition 2: 'The pharmacist must take all reasonable steps to prescribe contraceptives in accordance with the current online version of the section of the Therapeutic Guidelines titled 'Sexual and Reproductive Health: Contraception''.

Condition 3: 'The pharmacist may prescribe a medicine only at a premises that includes the relevant amenities and resources in the Amenities and resource requirements for the provision of hormonal contraceptive services detailed in this protocol.'

Amenities and resource requirements: 'A pharmacist must only act under the authority of this protocol when a private consulting area is used that: ensures patients' auditory and visual privacy and confidentiality; and has sufficient space to allow the presence of the following: the patient; a carer if necessary; the pharmacist undertaking the consultation; consumables; equipment; and documentation; and has seating for the patient and their carer during the consultation; and has hand washing facilities/hand sanitising products available to allow for the performance of appropriate hand hygiene before and after medication administration or examination of a patient. Appropriate equipment for patient examination'
Condition 4: 'When prescribing a medicine, the pharmacist must make a written prescription that is compliant with regulation 45 (Tas Poisons Regulations 2018).'

Condition 5: 'The pharmacist must, when prescribing the medicine, make an individualised clinical assessment of the patient's contraceptive and sexual health needs and suitability for hormonal contraception and management; and make and retain an electronic clinical record of the consultation with the patient, that includes: a) Relevant patient history and examination; and b) An assessment of the requirement for the prescribed medicine; and c) The management plan for treating the patient's condition including: i. The name of the medicine prescribed; and ii. The strength of the medicine prescribed; and iii. The formulation of the medicine prescribed; and iv. The instructions for use of the medicine prescribed; and v. The amount of the medicine prescribed.'
Condition 6: 'The pharmacist must not prescribe, in one prescription, greater than 12 months' supply of a medicine listed above in Condition 1.'
Protocol Overview - Meet service and professional obligations: 'Initial patient eligibility and suitability for management within the scope of the service'
Protocol Overview - Meet service and professional obligations: 'Patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant)'
'Service restricted to patients aged 16 years or over.'

Key Points: 'Patients are required to have a pharmacist consultation, including blood pressure (BP) and height and weight measurement (to calculate BMI), before a hormonal contraceptive method may be prescribed, regardless of whether the patient is currently using the type of contraception requested.'

Key Points: 'Before prescribing hormonal contraception, pharmacists should offer efficacy-based contraceptive counselling including discussing the use of LARCs with people seeking contraception, as per the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) recommendations.' (sentence spans pages 8-9)

Exclude pregnancy (page 11): 'Pregnancy should be reasonably excluded before commencing any hormonal contraception. A patient can be reasonably assumed not to be pregnant if: there are no symptoms or signs of pregnancy AND any of the following criteria are met:' - first limb: 'there are no symptoms or signs of pregnancy'.
Exclude pregnancy - any_of alternative 1: 'they have not had intercourse since the start of the last normal (natural) menstrual period, or since childbirth, abortion or miscarriage'

Exclude pregnancy - any_of alternative 2: 'they have been correctly and consistently using a reliable method of contraception (barrier methods can be assumed to be reliable if used correctly in this context)'
Exclude pregnancy - any_of alternative 3: 'they are within the first 5 days of the onset of a normal (natural) menstrual period or within the first 5 days after abortion or miscarriage'
Exclude pregnancy - any_of alternative 4: 'they are less than 21 days postpartum (non-lactating)'
Exclude pregnancy - any_of alternative 5: 'they have not had intercourse for >21 days and have a negative urine pregnancy test.'

exclusion.text: 'Refer when - Refer the patient to an appropriate healthcare provider (including sexual health service or emergency services, if required) in the following situations: The patient is younger than 16 years.'
'Refer when': 'the preferred contraceptive type is contraindicated or not appropriate (UKMEC 3 or 4).'
'Refer when': 'the patient requests or requires a method of contraception that is not available in the Hormonal Contraception Service e.g., long-acting reversible contraception (LARCs)'
'Refer when': 'the patient has unexplained vaginal bleeding, severe or painful menstrual bleeding, irregular periods, amenorrhea, or pain/discomfort with sexual intercourse'
'Refer when': 'the patient may be pregnant (refer to Exclude pregnancy)'
'Refer when': 'the patient has signs and symptoms of polycystic ovarian syndrome (PCOS) that have not been assessed by an appropriate healthcare provider'
'Refer when': 'the patient has undiagnosed hypertension, is hypertensive, or has poorly managed hypertension'

'Treat and concurrently refer promptly - Provide treatment and concurrently refer to an appropriate healthcare provider (including sexual health service or emergency services, if required) in the following situations: patient has been, or suspected to have been, subject to reproductive coercion, sexual abuse or sexual violence (refer to Reproductive coercion, sexual and domestic violence and abuse)'
'Treat and concurrently refer promptly': 'patient has symptoms of or risk factors for sexually transmitted infection (STI), or requests STI screening.'
'Treat and concurrently refer promptly': 'The Patient has a BMI of more than 35kg/m2'
'Treat and concurrently refer promptly': 'Patient has (or is suspected to have) endometriosis.'

Exclude pregnancy: 'If there is any doubt regarding whether the patient may be pregnant, even if a negative urine test is returned, hormonal contraception should NOT be prescribed and the patient referred to an appropriate healthcare provider.'
Medicines-level restriction (Condition 1a): combined hormonal contraception 'Excluding preparations containing 50 micrograms or more of ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol.'

Combined oral contraceptive (COC) pill: 'COCs containing 50 micrograms or more ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol, are NOT permitted for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service.' Restated page 15: 'COCs with a high estrogen dose (50 micrograms of ethinylestradiol or containing mestranol) are not routinely recommended for contraception because of the unacceptable risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). These formulations are not permitted for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service.'
Patient eligibility for combined hormonal contraception based on age (page 15): 'Patients aged 41 to 50 years: ... Do not initiate combined hormonal contraception in this age group.'

provenance.section_heading: Patient eligibility for combined hormonal contraception based on age

exclusion.text: Confirm contraceptive plan is appropriate: 'A hormonal contraception that is classified as UKMEC category of 3 or 4 for a patient CANNOT be prescribed as part of the Hormonal Contraception Service.'

exclusion_exceptions.text: Service banner (page 7): 'Ineligibility for treatment as part of a prescribing service does not preclude a patient from accessing services provided as part of usual pharmacy care.'

'Treat and concurrently refer promptly' (page 8): the four situations in that list are referral triggers but do not stop treatment - 'Provide treatment and concurrently refer to an appropriate healthcare provider (including sexual health service or emergency services, if required) in the following situations: ...' (patient remains treatable under the service while being referred).

Working with young people: 'People aged 16 and 17 years are generally assumed to have the capacity to consent to medical treatment (known as Gillick Competence), including for contraception, and consent from a parent/caregiver is not required (however, it is considered good practice for the parent/caregiver to be involved in decision making around health care). If the minor has the capacity to consent and does not wish to involve an adult, this should be respected.'

Contraceptive options for transgender and non-binary people: 'Current gender identity for transgender or non-binary people presumed female gender at birth does not impose any restrictions on methods of contraception that may be used. The same considerations apply for choosing safe and effective contraception, including personal characteristics, existing medical conditions and current drug therapies.'

provenance.section_heading: Contraceptive options for transgender and non-binary people

exclusion_exceptions.text: Age 41-50 continuation exception (page 15): 'Pharmacists may only prescribe continuation of existing combined hormonal contraception to patients in this age group. One original manufacturer's pack of combined hormonal contraception is permitted, and the patient concurrently referred to a general practitioner (or other medical practitioner where appropriate) for review and consideration of alternative contraceptive option.' (exception to the no-initiation rule in EXC-15, for continuation only).

provenance.section_heading: Patient eligibility for combined hormonal contraception based on age

exclusion_exceptions.text: Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection (page 16): 'DMPA may be the contraceptive of choice for individuals with contraindications to estrogen, those taking drugs that induce the CYP3A4 liver enzyme (refer to the Australian Medicines Handbook) or if a discrete method of contraception is preferred with less user input required.' (estrogen-related exclusions do not preclude DMPA).

Reproductive coercion, sexual and domestic violence and abuse (page 13): 'If emergency contraception (EC) is required, oral EC may be supplied as per usual pharmacy care.' (oral EC is supplied as usual pharmacy care rather than under this prescribing protocol).

provenance.section_heading: Reproductive coercion, sexual and domestic violence and abuse

steps.description: 'Meet service and professional obligations: Initial patient eligibility and suitability for management within the scope of the service; Patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant).'

gates.criterion: Initial patient eligibility and suitability for management within the scope of the service
Patient informed consent (including consent for communication with other health practitioners if relevant)

steps.description: 'Patient history and assessment: Patient medical history incl. (Sexual, reproductive and social history); Sexual and reproduction health counselling; Exclude pregnancy; Examination (Body mass index (BMI); Blood pressure measurement).' Exclude-pregnancy decision is detailed in PW-2.

gates.criterion: Pregnancy reasonably excluded before commencing hormonal contraception (see PW-2)

steps.description: 'Contraceptive and sexual health plan: Discuss LARCs; Select appropriate contraceptive option - Combined oral contraceptive pill; Combined hormonal vaginal ring; Progestogen-only contraceptive pill; Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA).' (Key Points, page 8: the service 'allows for the prescription of four types of hormonal contraception').

gates.criterion: Selected option is one of the four hormonal contraceptive types available in the Hormonal Contraception Service (COC, combined hormonal vaginal ring, POP, DMPA)

steps.description: 'Confirm contraception plan is appropriate: UKMEC; Contraindications, precautions and interactions; Pregnancy and lactation.' (detailed decision rules in PW-3).

gates.criterion: Chosen contraception confirmed appropriate (UKMEC; contraindications, precautions and interactions; pregnancy and lactation)

steps.description: 'Communicate agreed contraception plan: Medication counselling; General advice and patient information; Communication with other health practitioners.' (detailed counselling content on page 18, see PW-4-S1).
'Clinical review: Measure BP and BMI; Adverse effects; Continue, change or stop contraception; Communication with other health professionals.'

'Pregnancy should be reasonably excluded before commencing any hormonal contraception. A patient can be reasonably assumed not to be pregnant if: there are no symptoms or signs of pregnancy AND any of the following criteria are met:'.

gates.criterion: No symptoms or signs of pregnancy

steps.description: Second limb of the same rule - at least one of: 'they have not had intercourse since the start of the last normal (natural) menstrual period, or since childbirth, abortion or miscarriage'; OR 'they have been correctly and consistently using a reliable method of contraception (barrier methods can be assumed to be reliable if used correctly in this context)'; OR 'they are within the first 5 days of the onset of a normal (natural) menstrual period or within the first 5 days after abortion or miscarriage'; OR 'they are less than 21 days postpartum (non-lactating)'; OR 'they have not had intercourse for >21 days and have a negative urine pregnancy test.'

gates.criterion: At least one of the five printed conditions is met (any_of)

steps.description: 'Use of an appropriate pregnancy test is recommended - this may include referral for a blood test for serum human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG) levels.'

'If there is any doubt regarding whether the patient may be pregnant, even if a negative urine test is returned, hormonal contraception should NOT be prescribed and the patient referred to an appropriate healthcare provider.'

gates.criterion: No doubt remains about whether the patient may be pregnant (including after a negative urine test)

diagnosis_pathways.name: Patient assessment, selection and confirmation of the hormonal contraceptive option (pages 9-18)

steps.description: 'Initial consultation - An individualised assessment of contraceptive and sexual health needs and suitability for hormonal contraception and management within the Service should consider: patient medical history including sexual, reproductive and social history; discussion of all available contraceptive options (including options not available in the Service that may be more suitable and available on referral); assessment of medical eligibility and contraindications; BP and height measurement and BMI calculation; risk assessment for STIs.'

'Selection of an appropriate hormonal method and formulation should consider: factors that could affect contraceptive effectiveness (including product efficacy); how long the patient thinks they will be using contraception (e.g. less than 1 year, fewer than 3 years, more than 3 years); non-contraceptive benefits; common side effects and risk of adverse effects; health risks and individualised advice. Comprehensive counselling and advice may include: the use of tailored regimens; starting hormonal contraception without delay (Quick Start); avoiding contraceptive failure, including instructions on missed pills.' 'For detailed information on each contraceptive option, including contraindications and precautions, pharmacists should consult the Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health, current guidance from ... RANZCOG and ... RCOG College of Sexual and Reproductive Healthcare (CoSRH) ... including: UK Medical Eligibility Criteria for Contraceptive Use (UKMEC); CoSRH/FSHR Clinical guideline - Progestogen-only Pills; CoSRH/FSHR Clinical guideline - Combined Hormonal Contraception; CoSRH/FSHR Clinical guideline - Progestogen-only injectable contraception; RANZCOG Contraception clinical guideline.'

'Patient history - Obtain sufficient information from the patient to assess the safety and appropriateness of any recommendations and medicines. The patient history should consider: age; gender assigned at birth and fertility status (for transgender and non-binary patients); plans to become pregnant, current pregnancy status (and how this has been determined); recent pregnancies, and lactation status; underlying medical conditions including mental health conditions, which may be a contraindication to hormonal contraception as per UKMEC criteria e.g. migraine, liver or heart disease, clotting conditions; current and recently ceased treatments (including prescribed medicines, vitamins, herbs, other supplements, and over-the-counter medicines); drug allergies/adverse reactions; prior use of contraceptives, tolerability and adverse effects including mood-related symptoms; smoking status; BMI; other factors such as age of menarche, usual menstrual cycle, heavy periods, period pain or changes in menstrual cycle, irregular or post-coital bleeding, symptoms that may suggest endometriosis (e.g. pelvic pain, severe pain with menstruation and/or sexual intercourse), symptoms that may suggest PCOS (e.g. infrequent periods, hirsutism, acne, weight gain); last STI screen and Cervical Screening Test (CST); presence of genitourinary symptoms that may suggest an STI: changes in vaginal or urethral discharge, vulval, genital skin problems or symptoms, lower abdominal pain, dysuria; Human Papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination status.'

'Sexual, reproductive and social history - In addition to a standard patient history, pharmacists should also take a social, sexual and reproductive history from the patient to inform shared decision making. When taking a sexual history: Start by asking open questions about the patient's social background (to enable the patient to relax and provide the appropriate context for decision-making). More specific questions can then be asked about risk behaviours, followed by questions around sexual practices if required. The following issues should be considered to determine if the patient is at risk of an STI, or if STI testing is indicated, but may not be relevant to all people: previous use and experiences with contraception including EC.'

Continuation of the STI-risk issue list (page 11, no printed heading above this block): 'current relationship status; number of recent partners and their gender; risky behaviours including illicit and/or intravenous drug use, alcohol use; potential for reproductive coercion, sexual and domestic abuse (refer to Reproductive coercion, sexual and domestic violence and abuse); previous STIs and risk factors for STIs (including STI history of current and/or recent partner if applicable); Previous unplanned pregnancies'. 'Reminder: Pharmacists can access a range of clinical information in a patient's My Health Record, including details about current and past medication history, allergies and current medical conditions.'

'Examination - The pharmacist should measure BP, weight and height and calculate BMI to determine the patient's suitability for their preferred contraceptive type, and to monitor potential impacts of contraception, including hypertension. BP should be measured in accordance with the National Heart Foundation of Australia Guideline for the diagnosis and management of hypertension in adults. A single elevated BP reading is not enough to classify a patient as hypertensive, and a second BP reading should be taken at the end of the consultation.'

gates.criterion: Patient is not hypertensive on BP assessment (a single elevated reading is not enough to classify a patient as hypertensive; a second BP reading is taken at the end of the consultation)

steps.description: 'Selecting the most appropriate hormonal contraceptive option - Pharmacists must ensure that they are prescribing medicines according to the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines in accordance with Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexual and Reproductive Health (Contraception) (21). The UK MEC calculator should be used to ensure all possible contraindications are considered prior to prescribing.'

provenance.section_heading: Selecting the most appropriate hormonal contraceptive option

steps.description: 'Pharmacists may prescribe a hormonal contraception with MEC 1 or 2 but should refer individuals to an alternative prescriber if their preferred choice of contraception is MEC 3 or 4.'

gates.criterion: Preferred choice of contraception is MEC 1 or 2

provenance.section_heading: Selecting the most appropriate hormonal contraceptive option

steps.description: 'The choice of hormonal contraception will depend on: the patient's history; the patient's preference: cost (short and long term), ease of use, management of other conditions, potential side effects; contraceptive efficacy: When used correctly, the hormonal methods available in the Hormonal Contraception Service have similar failure rates. However, the consistency of user adherence required is variable, and this may impact on effectiveness. LARC methods (IUDs and implants) are the most reliable and cost-effective reversible methods of contraception. Pharmacists should not assume effectiveness is the only factor in an individual's choice of contraception, but they should explain relative efficacy to patients.'

provenance.section_heading: Selecting the most appropriate hormonal contraceptive option

steps.description: 'Patient eligibility for combined hormonal contraception based on age - Patients aged 16 to 40 years: Eligible for the prescription of combined hormonal contraception (this includes initiation and continuation). Patients aged 41 to 50 years: Pharmacists may only prescribe continuation of existing combined hormonal contraception to patients in this age group. One original manufacturer's pack of combined hormonal contraception is permitted, and the patient concurrently referred to a general practitioner (or other medical practitioner where appropriate) for review and consideration of alternative contraceptive option. Do not initiate combined hormonal contraception in this age group.'

gates.criterion: If aged 41 to 50 years: continuation only of existing combined hormonal contraception with one original manufacturer's pack and concurrent GP review (no initiation)

provenance.section_heading: Patient eligibility for combined hormonal contraception based on age

steps.description: 'Confirm contraceptive plan is appropriate - Consult the current editions of the Therapeutic Guidelines, the Australian Medicines Handbook, and the UKMEC Guidelines or calculator to confirm contraceptive management is appropriate, including for: contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and lactation. A hormonal contraception that is classified as UKMEC category of 3 or 4 for a patient CANNOT be prescribed as part of the Hormonal Contraception Service.'

gates.criterion: Chosen hormonal contraception is not classified as UKMEC category 3 or 4

diagnosis_pathways.name: Communicate plan, clinical review and issuing a prescription (pages 18-20)

steps.description: 'Communicate agreed contraceptive plan - Comprehensive advice and counselling (including supporting written information when required) should be provided to the patient regarding: individual product and medicine use (instructions for commencing; deviation from schedule (e.g. a pill is missed, a DMPA injection is not administered at 12 weeks, or a new vaginal ring is inserted too late or removed before the 3-week interval); how long a secondary method of contraception must be used to avoid unplanned pregnancy; instructions on tailored regimens; advice on when fertility can be expected to return after ceasing the contraceptive); emergency contraceptive options that are available in instances of contraceptive failure; how to manage adverse effects; when to seek further care and/or treatment (signs of VTE and what to do if it is suspected; the importance of reporting new or worsening mood-related symptoms); review with an appropriate healthcare provider at least every 2 years; when to return for follow-up.'
'The agreed management plan should be shared with the patient and members of their multidisciplinary healthcare team, with the patient's consent.'

gates.criterion: Patient consent to share the agreed management plan with members of their multidisciplinary healthcare team

steps.description: 'Clinical review with the pharmacist (or the patient's chosen healthcare provider) should occur in line with recommendations in the Therapeutic Guidelines. Patients should be instructed to seek a follow up consultation 3 months after initiation of a new contraceptive method (i.e. the patient has no recent experience of taking that type of contraception) to screen for adverse effects including hypertension. To facilitate this, best practice prescribing would not include a repeat on the initial prescription for a new hormonal contraceptive method.'

Clinical review continuation (page 20, no printed heading above this block): 'Clinical review, including measurement of the patient's BP and reviewing contraindications, is recommended at 12 monthly intervals for all patients on regular contraceptive. For patients continuing therapy, follow-up should be individualised to the patient's clinical presentation, response to treatment, and therapeutic goals. Pharmacists should prescribe a quantity of medicine (including repeats), that aligns with the expected duration of therapy, ensuring sufficient supply until the patient's next review. The total quantity prescribed is not to exceed 12 months' supply (including repeats).'

'Issuing a prescription - Pharmacists are to issue a prescription for any supply of hormonal contraception. Prescribing may only be undertaken by pharmacists who have completed approved training and maintained appropriate continuing professional development. Any prescription needs to comply with Regulation 45 of the Tasmanian Poisons Regulations 2018 ... Electronic prescribing templates may be used, provided they meet the requirements of Reg 45 and are signed in ink by the pharmacist. Pharmacists are to indicate the words "authorised health professional" after their signature and name on the prescription. The original prescription is to accompany any repeats and the pharmacy is to establish a process to record prescribing details on file. Pharmacists in Tasmania will not be provided with, or be required to use, a prescriber number. Patients MUST be provided with the option of having their prescription filled at the pharmacy of their choice.'

'Dispensing (when same pharmacy as prescribing): Dispensing process is to be performed separately from prescribing (for example: physically move from consult room into the dispensary). Best practice advice: wherever available, another pharmacy staff member should be involved in the dispensing process. A pharmacist (first-preference) or a dispense tech.'

'Working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people - Sexual health is not openly discussed in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures and shame may be a strong barrier to seeking sexual health care or contraception, especially in smaller communities. All health care providers should be cognisant of causing additional shame ... Pharmacists should consult the Department of Health Aboriginal health and cultural respect and the Pharmaceutical Society of Australia's Guideline for Pharmacists supporting Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples with Medicines Management ... Where appropriate, Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health workers or health practitioners may be involved to support clients with contraception self-management and facilitate the provision of a culturally safe service by the pharmacist.'

provenance.section_heading: Working with Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander people

steps.description: 'Working with young people - Although a pharmacist may prescribe a hormonal contraception to an individual from age 16 years, people younger than 16 are to be confidentially referred to an appropriate health care provider or sexual health clinic.'

gates.criterion: Patient is 16 years of age or older

steps.description: 'Working with young people - People aged 16 and 17 years are generally assumed to have the capacity to consent to medical treatment (known as Gillick Competence), including for contraception, and consent from a parent/caregiver is not required ... To assess the minor's capacity to consent to treatment, healthcare providers must consider the minor's capacity to understand the risks and benefits of the contraception (and the seriousness of the risks of using hormonal contraception and not using contraception) to make an informed decision. Assessments of capacity to consent for minors (or adults where competency may be in doubt, for example people with an intellectual disability) must be documented in the patient record.'

'If the pharmacist cannot determine the minor's capacity, they should refer the patient to an appropriate healthcare provider for further assessment. Youth Health Services provide a range of free health services and programs for young people aged 12 to 24 years in Tasmania.'

gates.criterion: The minor's capacity to consent can be determined by the pharmacist

steps.description: 'Working with young people - Pharmacists should consider whether there may be child protection concerns relating to a request for contraception and report to Child Safety accordingly. More information is available on the Strong Families Safe Kids website.'

gates.criterion: No child protection concerns relating to the request for contraception

steps.description: 'Reproductive coercion, sexual and domestic violence and abuse - Pharmacists should be aware of the possibility that a person seeking contraception may be and/or may have been subjected to reproductive coercion, sexual violence or abuse ... If the pharmacist becomes aware of this during the consultation, they should provide appropriate trauma-informed support and assistance, including referral to support options depending on the patient circumstances. Referral options include to the local hospital, sexual health clinic and/or community-based sexual violence support services. A list of services, including sexual assault and domestic violence helplines and local services is provided on the Tasmanian Government Community Family Violence and Sexual Assault webpage. 1800 RESPECT (1800 737 732) is a 24-hour national sexual assault, family and domestic violence counselling line for any Australian who has experienced, or is at risk of, family and domestic violence and/or sexual assault.'

provenance.section_heading: Reproductive coercion, sexual and domestic violence and abuse

steps.description: 'If emergency contraception (EC) is required, oral EC may be supplied as per usual pharmacy care. Ulipristal is the most effective oral form of EC, however the most appropriate oral EC for a patient depends on several factors including whether or not a hormonal contraception was used in the 7 days leading up to the request for EC or is planned to commence in the 5 days following provision of EC. (refer to Therapeutic Guidelines - Sexual and Reproductive Health). Insertion of a copper intrauterine device (IUD) is overall the most effective form of EC. The patient may require referral to an appropriate medical practitioner or health service for IUD insertion.'

provenance.section_heading: Reproductive coercion, sexual and domestic violence and abuse

steps.description: 'Contraceptive options for transgender and non-binary people - Transgender and non-binary people may benefit from referral to specialist sexual health services for comprehensive and culturally safe sexual healthcare that is tailored to their individual needs. Tasmanian sexual health clinics and outreach services are located across Tasmania ... The use of inclusive and non-gendered language during a consultation is encouraged ... Current gender identity ... does not impose any restrictions on methods of contraception that may be used ... Information on cervical screening should be provided to transgender men and non-binary people who have a uterus.'

provenance.section_heading: Contraceptive options for transgender and non-binary people

steps.description: 'Patients over 50 years of age - The choice of contraceptive should be reconsidered at age 50 and at menopause. Contraception is required for 12 months after the final menstrual period if it occurs after the age of 50. If the final menstrual period occurs before the age of 50, 24 months of contraception is required before cessation. Some methods of contraception are not suitable for certain age groups; more information is provided below.' (page 14).

treatments.notes: Condition 1(a) (page 5): 'Combined hormonal contraception - combined oral contraceptive pills (COCs) and the contraceptive vaginal ring. Excluding preparations containing 50 micrograms or more of ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol.' Choice of COC (page 15): 'The COC with the lowest effective dose of estrogen and progestogen that is well tolerated and able to provide acceptable menstrual cycle control for the patient should be chosen as first-line.'; 'Other guiding principles for COC pill selection are: safety profile, affordability and additional non-contraceptive benefits if desired.'; 'Newer progestogens reduce the potential for androgenic, estrogenic and glucocorticoid effects.'; 'The quadriphasic pill is indicated for heavy menstrual bleeding as well as contraception but it has complex instructions for managing a missed pill.'; 'Triphasic pills are no longer commonly used because of a lack of benefits over other types.'; 'The COCs available in Australia and for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service are listed in the Therapeutic Guidelines: Formulations of combined hormonal contraception table.'; 'COCs with a high estrogen dose (50 micrograms of ethinylestradiol or containing mestranol) are not routinely recommended for contraception because of the unacceptable risk of venous thromboembolism (VTE). These formulations are not permitted for use in the Hormonal Contraception Service.' Age limits (page 15): initiation only at ages 16-40; ages 41-50 continuation only with one original manufacturer's pack and concurrent GP review. Pregnancy/lactation caveat (page 18, verbatim): confirm management including for 'contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and lactation.' No dose, frequency or duration is printed - regimens are delegated to 'the current online version of the section of the Therapeutic Guidelines titled Sexual and Reproductive Health: Contraception' (Condition 2, page 5). Supply limit (page 20): 'The total quantity prescribed is not to exceed 12 months' supply (including repeats).'

Condition 1(a) (page 5) includes 'the contraceptive vaginal ring' within combined hormonal contraception, with the same exclusion: 'Excluding preparations containing 50 micrograms or more of ethinylestradiol, or preparations containing mestranol.' Page 16: 'Patients that require assistance with insertion of a vaginal ring should be referred to an appropriate healthcare provider.' Deviation-from-schedule counselling (page 18, verbatim): 'a new vaginal ring is inserted too late or removed before the 3-week interval'. No dose, frequency or duration is printed (delegated to Therapeutic Guidelines, Condition 2 page 5). Supply limit (page 20): 'The total quantity prescribed is not to exceed 12 months' supply (including repeats).'

Condition 1(b) (page 5): 'Progestogen-only contraceptive pill'. Choice of POP (page 16): 'For patients who have a contraindication to estrogen in COC pills or prefer estrogen-free contraception, POPs can be considered. Drospirenone provides more consistent suppression of ovulation than levonorgestrel or norethisterone and may provide better bleeding control.' Reference (page 16): 'Refer to: RANZCOG & FSRH Contraception Clinical Guideline and FSRH Clinical guideline: Progestogen-only Pills.' Pregnancy/lactation caveat (page 18, verbatim): confirm management including for 'contraindications and precautions; drug interactions; pregnancy and lactation.' No dose, frequency or duration is printed (delegated to Therapeutic Guidelines, Condition 2 page 5). Supply limit (page 20): 'The total quantity prescribed is not to exceed 12 months' supply (including repeats).'

Condition 1(c) (page 5): 'Depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (injection)'. Key Points (page 8): 'depot medroxyprogesterone acetate (DMPA) injection (including administration of the injection)'. Page 16: 'DMPA may be the contraceptive of choice for individuals with contraindications to estrogen, those taking drugs that induce the CYP3A4 liver enzyme (refer to the Australian Medicines Handbook) or if a discrete method of contraception is preferred with less user input required.'; 'DMPA is not a first-line option for adolescents or in perimenopausal patients because of the theoretical propensity to cause bone mineral density (BMD) loss and/or limit peak BMD.'; 'During each consultation, pharmacists should assess the user's risk factors for low BMD and cardiovascular disease.'; 'Patients who wish to continue using DMPA should be reviewed by an appropriate healthcare provider every 2 years to assess any changes in benefits and potential risks of use.'; 'Pharmacists should be familiar with the small but significant association between prolonged use of DMPA and intracranial meningioma a rare and predominantly benign tumour. See: FSRH CEU Statement: Response to new study CoSRH.' Paediatric caveat verbatim (page 16): 'DMPA is not a first-line option for adolescents...' Injection route/site/volume are not printed. No dose, frequency or duration is printed (delegated to Therapeutic Guidelines, Condition 2 page 5); missed-injection counselling (page 18): 'a DMPA injection is not administered at 12 weeks'. Supply limit (page 20): 'The total quantity prescribed is not to exceed 12 months' supply (including repeats).'

Supplied as usual pharmacy care, not under this prescribing protocol (page 13): 'If emergency contraception (EC) is required, oral EC may be supplied as per usual pharmacy care. Ulipristal is the most effective oral form of EC, however the most appropriate oral EC for a patient depends on several factors including whether or not a hormonal contraception was used in the 7 days leading up to the request for EC or is planned to commence in the 5 days following provision of EC. (refer to Therapeutic Guidelines - Sexual and Reproductive Health).' Also page 13: 'Insertion of a copper intrauterine device (IUD) is overall the most effective form of EC. The patient may require referral to an appropriate medical practitioner or health service for IUD insertion.' No product strengths, doses, intervals or quantities are printed for any EC product; all EC selection/dosing is delegated to the Therapeutic Guidelines - see open_questions.

open_questions.observed: Page 17 shows only the footer line 'Tasmanian Community Pharmacist Program Clinical Practice Protocol – Hormonal Contraception Page 17'. The Contents (pages 2-3) assign 'Confirm contraceptive plan is appropriate...17' and 'Communicate agreed contraception plan...17' to page 17, but both headings appear under the === PAGE 18 === marker in the extraction.
open_questions.why_unclear: Page 17 may contain an image/figure or a text layer that did not extract; no structured claim could be attributed to page 17. Content-bearing claims for those two sections were taken from page 18 where the headings actually appear.

open_questions.topic: Contents page numbers drift from the actual page markers
open_questions.observed: Contents lists 'Confirm contraception plan is appropriate...17', 'Communicate agreed contraception plan...17', 'Clinical review...19', 'Issuing a prescription...19' while the extracted headings appear on pages 18, 18, 19-20 and 20 respectively; Contents also lists 'Other considerations...17' while the heading appears on page 18.
open_questions.why_unclear: Printed contents numbers are stale relative to the page markers; the spec requires page markers as the only valid page source, so all provenance uses marker pages.

open_questions.topic: No dose, frequency, duration, strength or quantity figures printed for any medicine
open_questions.observed: Condition 1 (page 5) names the three medicine classes only; regimens are delegated: 'The pharmacist must take all reasonable steps to prescribe contraceptives in accordance with the current online version of the section of the Therapeutic Guidelines titled Sexual and Reproductive Health: Contraception' and page 14 'Pharmacists must ensure that they are prescribing medicines according to the specified sections of the current online version of the Therapeutic Guidelines'. The only quantity rule is 'The total quantity prescribed is not to exceed 12 months' supply (including repeats).' (page 20).
open_questions.why_unclear: All dose/frequency/duration/max fields are left empty by design; no values were invented. EC doses (page 13) are also delegated to the Therapeutic Guidelines.

open_questions.topic: No class-level first-line ranking among the four permitted methods
open_questions.observed: The only 'first-line' statement is within COC selection (page 15): 'The COC with the lowest effective dose of estrogen and progestogen ... should be chosen as first-line.' The document does not rank COC vs ring vs POP vs DMPA.
open_questions.why_unclear: first_line is false on all five treatment rows because no method-level first-line statement exists; do not read this as a ranking.

open_questions.observed: Page 11: 'A patient can be reasonably assumed not to be pregnant if: there are no symptoms or signs of pregnancy AND any of the following criteria are met: ...' followed by five bullets.
open_questions.why_unclear: Encoded as criteria_group {all_of: [INC-13], any_of: [INC-14..INC-18]} following the printed AND/any wording; the document states the combinatorics explicitly so confidence is high.

open_questions.topic: 'Treat and concurrently refer promptly' has no matching action in the schema
open_questions.observed: Page 8: 'Provide treatment and concurrently refer to an appropriate healthcare provider ... in the following situations:' for four situations (reproductive coercion/sexual abuse; STI symptoms, risk factors or screening request; BMI more than 35kg/m2; suspected endometriosis).
open_questions.why_unclear: The schema action enum has no TREAT_AND_REFER value, so RF-8..RF-11 use action REFER with the concurrent-treatment wording preserved verbatim in trigger_text; EXE-2 records that treatment continues.

open_questions.topic: Child Safety reporting has no matching action in the schema
open_questions.observed: Page 12: 'Pharmacists should consider whether there may be child protection concerns relating to a request for contraception and report to Child Safety accordingly.'
open_questions.why_unclear: The action enum has no REPORT value; RF-15 and PW-5-S5 are encoded as REFER with confidence 'medium' because it is a statutory reporting duty, not a healthcare-provider referral. See hugh_to_confirm.

open_questions.observed: Several blocks continue from the previous page with no printed heading above them on their own page: page 6 (training section continuation before 'Amenities and resource requirements'), page 11 (STI-risk issue list before 'Reminder'), page 13 (first block continues page 12 abuse section before 'Contraceptive options for transgender and non-binary people'), page 16 (age-eligibility bullets before 'Combined hormonal vaginal ring'), page 19 (VTE bullets before 'Contraception and cancer risks'), page 20 (Clinical review bullets before 'Issuing a prescription').
open_questions.why_unclear: section_heading is set to '' for those blocks per the spec ('Use "" only if the page truly has no heading'); the carried section name is quoted in the step/criterion text instead.

open_questions.topic: Emergency services destination is conditional with no emergency-specific trigger
open_questions.observed: Both page 8 list introductions say 'including sexual health service or emergency services, if required'; no situation in the document is designated emergency-only, and no 000/ambulance instruction is printed.
open_questions.why_unclear: referral.emergency contains only the conditional quote; no emergency trigger was invented.

open_questions.topic: Protocol Overview box (page 7) vs the detailed lists (page 8) differ slightly
open_questions.observed: The page 7 'Refer when' box reads 'The patient is hypertensive, or has poorly managed hypertension' (page 8 adds 'undiagnosed') and does not include 'The patient is younger than 16 years.'; the page 7 box also words the pregnancy item as 'The patient may be pregnant'.
open_questions.why_unclear: Both readings recorded: exclusion/red-flag items were built from the complete page 8 lists; the page 7 box appears verbatim inside the PW-1 overview steps.

open_questions.observed: Example: the Key Points efficacy-counselling sentence starts on page 8 ('...discussing the use of LARCs with people seeking') and finishes on page 9 ('contraception, as per the Royal Australian and New Zealand College of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists (RANZCOG) recommendations.'); the patient-history list also runs from page 10 to 11.
open_questions.why_unclear: Provenance uses the page where the sentence begins; the full wording is quoted in the criterion/step text and the span is noted here.

open_questions.observed: Documentation/notification duties appear on pages 5 (electronic clinical record), 11 (My Health Record), 12 (capacity documentation; Child Safety reporting), 18 (management plan sharing with consent) and 20 (prescription record on file).
open_questions.why_unclear: One shared provenance object references the first page (5); each condition carries its own page reference inline.

open_questions.observed: Page 8 says the service includes 'administration of the injection' but no route, site, volume, needle or reconstitution detail appears anywhere in the document.
open_questions.why_unclear: route field left empty on TX-4; no administration detail invented (delegated to external guidelines).

open_questions.topic: No upper age bound for the service
open_questions.observed: Only a minimum is printed: 'Service restricted to patients aged 16 years or over.' (page 7) and 'patient aged 16 years or older' (page 5). Page 13 gives over-50 contraception-duration advice rather than an age cap; combined hormonal contraception has its own 41-50 initiation restriction (page 15).
open_questions.why_unclear: age_bounds.max_years is null; over-50 handling is captured in PW-5-S9 and EXC-15/EXE-5 instead.

open_questions.topic: Review-interval wording differs between counselling and clinical review sections
open_questions.observed: Page 18 counselling: 'review with an appropriate healthcare provider at least every 2 years'; page 20 clinical review: 'recommended at 12 monthly intervals for all patients on regular contraceptive'; DMPA continuation: 'reviewed by an appropriate healthcare provider every 2 years' (page 16).
open_questions.why_unclear: All three intervals recorded separately in review_followup with their own provenance; the document does not reconcile them (2-yearly review is the counselling message, 12-monthly is the clinical-review recommendation).

open_questions.topic: UKMEC categories are required but no category table is printed
open_questions.observed: Pages 14 and 18 require 'The UK MEC calculator' and 'the UKMEC Guidelines or calculator' and set the MEC 1/2 prescribe vs MEC 3/4 refer rule, but the document prints no UKMEC category definitions.
open_questions.why_unclear: Red flags RF-2, RF-19 and RF-24 therefore carry structured: null; the category values must come from the external UKMEC tool.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Approved training: 'a hormonal contraception training program that meets criteria defined by this protocol' - delivered by 'a higher education institution accredited by the Tertiary Education Quality and Standards Agency' or 'a training provider that meets the Australian Pharmacy Council's Standards for Continuing Professional Development Activities', covering the listed learning objectives and the National Prescribing Service 'Prescribing Competencies Framework' items (pages 5-6).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Per-pharmacist training certificates must be verified against the protocol criteria before go-live; no named approved course list is printed in this document.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Premises approval: 'Pharmacists must only offer this structured prescribing service in a pharmacy premises that has been approved for this purpose by the Department of Health' plus the private-consulting-area amenities checklist (pages 4 and 6).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Approval status must be confirmed per site, and the amenities/privacy/equipment checklist evidenced locally.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Prescription formalities: 'Any prescription needs to comply with Regulation 45 of the Tasmanian Poisons Regulations 2018 ... signed in ink by the pharmacist. Pharmacists are to indicate the words "authorised health professional" after their signature and name on the prescription. The original prescription is to accompany any repeats and the pharmacy is to establish a process to record prescribing details on file. Pharmacists in Tasmania will not be provided with, or be required to use, a prescriber number.' (page 20)
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Local prescribing workflow, template configuration and record-retention process must be validated against Reg 45 before go-live.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Supply cap: Condition 6 'The pharmacist must not prescribe, in one prescription, greater than 12 months' supply' and page 20 'The total quantity prescribed is not to exceed 12 months' supply (including repeats).'
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Quantity/repeat limits must be configured in the prescribing and dispensing system.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Professional discretion clause (page 7): 'When applying the information contained within this clinical practice protocol, pharmacists are advised to exercise professional discretion and judgement. The clinical practice protocol does not override the responsibility of the pharmacist to make decisions appropriate to the circumstances of the individual, in consultation with the patient and/or their parent/caregiver.'
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Open-ended discretion clause; needs a local policy boundary before enforcement by a rules engine.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Electronic clinical record minimum dataset (Condition 5, page 5): history and examination; assessment of requirement; management plan with name, strength, formulation, instructions for use and amount of medicine prescribed.
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Clinical software must be configured to capture every listed element, plus consent for communication (page 7) and capacity documentation (page 12).

hugh_to_confirm.item: External reference currency: 'current online version of the section of the Therapeutic Guidelines titled Sexual and Reproductive Health: Contraception' (page 5); 'The UK MEC calculator should be used' (page 14); 'Consult the current editions of the Therapeutic Guidelines, the Australian Medicines Handbook, and the UKMEC Guidelines or calculator' (page 18).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Rules depend on external, versioned references; confirm which versions the module pins at go-live.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Age 41-50 combined hormonal contraception rule: 'Pharmacists may only prescribe continuation of existing combined hormonal contraception ... One original manufacturer's pack of combined hormonal contraception is permitted, and the patient concurrently referred ... Do not initiate combined hormonal contraception in this age group.' (page 15)
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Initiation block and one-pack quantity limit must be configured; 'existing' (how long established) is not defined in the document.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Capacity/consent for minors: Gillick Competence for 16-17 year olds; 'To assess the minor's capacity to consent to treatment, healthcare providers must consider the minor's capacity ... Assessments of capacity to consent for minors ... must be documented in the patient record.' (page 12)
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Capacity assessment is case-by-case; local documentation standard required.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Child Safety reporting: 'Pharmacists should consider whether there may be child protection concerns relating to a request for contraception and report to Child Safety accordingly.' (page 12)
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Statutory reporting duty with no printed threshold; encoded as REFER because the schema has no report action - local policy must define the decision path and record.

hugh_to_confirm.item: Emergency contraception outside the protocol: 'If emergency contraception (EC) is required, oral EC may be supplied as per usual pharmacy care. Ulipristal is the most effective oral form of EC ...' and copper IUD referral (page 13).
hugh_to_confirm.reason: Confirm what 'usual pharmacy care' covers under this service, and how product choice (ulipristal vs levonorgestrel) is governed, since no EC doses are printed here.

hugh_to_confirm.item: DMPA-specific duties: 'During each consultation, pharmacists should assess the user's risk factors for low BMD and cardiovascular disease'; 'reviewed by an appropriate healthcare provider every 2 years'; 'Pharmacists should be familiar with the small but significant association between prolonged use of DMPA and intracranial meningioma ...' (page 16).
